additions.title: Guidelines on the implementation of the transparency obligations for certain AI systems under Article 50 of the AI Act, C(2026) 5054 final, Annex
additions.locator: Section 4.2, paragraph 70; marking obligation defined at 4.2.1, paragraph 71
additions.quote: For every marking solution deployed, providers should ensure that corresponding means for detection are available
additions.why: The Commission's reading of the marking duty: two linked elements, marking and detectability, and marking without a way to detect it 'will not suffice'. Supports 'detection capability maintained' in the top level. Non-binding; content approved 20 July 2026 with formal adoption to follow once all language versions exist. The PDF itself, linked from the Commission's library page.

additions.title: California Senate Bill No. 942 (California AI Transparency Act), Chapter 291, Statutes of 2024
additions.locator: Section 1, adding Business and Professions Code s.22757.3(b)
additions.quote: A covered provider shall include a latent disclosure in AI-generated image, video, or audio content
additions.why: Comparator: a US state statute that requires a machine-readable ('latent') mark, an optional visible one (s.22757.3(a)) and a free public detection tool (s.22757.2). Text is not among the content types listed. Applies only to generative systems with over 1,000,000 monthly users. Chaptered text as enacted in 2024; later amendments and the operative date were not checked. US state law.

additions.title: Reducing Risks Posed by Synthetic Content: An Overview of Technical Approaches to Digital Content Transparency (NIST AI 100-4)
additions.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
additions.quote: none of these techniques can be considered as a comprehensive solution; the value of any given technique is use-case and context specific
additions.why: The fullest public technical survey of watermarking, metadata and detection, with the known ways each fails (compression, cropping, paraphrase). Evidence for layered marking and for testing robustness instead of trusting a supplier. A technical overview, not a standard or a rule; US federal agency.

additions.title: Content Credentials: C2PA Technical Specification, version 2.4
additions.publisher: Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA)
additions.quote: A digitally signed and tamper-evident data structure that references a set of assertions
additions.why: The open industry specification for signed provenance metadata, the kind of 'digitally signed metadata' the EU code asks for as one layer. Free to read. An industry consortium specification, not a formal national or international standard on the page read; the research log records that the EU code does not name it. Version 2.4 (April 2026) was the latest found; check for a newer one.

additions.title: Public content provenance for organisations
additions.publisher: National Cyber Security Centre and Canadian Centre for Cyber Security
additions.quote: Digital watermarking is not a provenance mechanism but is included here because it is often considered for addressing digital trust challenges.
additions.why: The UK's technical authority on what provenance tools can and cannot prove. Useful corrective: a watermark shows a signal is present, not where content came from, so it complements signed metadata and does not replace it. A primer for security and communications teams, written for organisations proving their own content is genuine, not for marking AI output; no duty attached. Date taken from the NCSC collection page.

additions.title: Artificial Intelligence Playbook for the UK Government
additions.locator: Principle 7 (You are open and collaborative), practical recommendations
additions.quote: Clearly signpost when AI has been used to create content, is interacting with members of the public, or is used in decision-making processes
additions.why: The nearest thing to a UK labelling expectation: government tells its own departments to signpost AI-made content. Visible signposting only; says nothing about machine-readable marks. Public-sector guidance, not a duty on companies.

additions.title: A Watermark for Large Language Models
additions.publisher: Kirchenbauer, Geiping, Wen, Katz, Miers and Goldstein, arXiv:2301.10226 (ICML 2023)
additions.quote: embedding signals into generated text that are invisible to humans but algorithmically detectable from a short span of tokens
additions.why: The paper that set out how text watermarking works in practice, and the basis for much of what the EU code calls an imperceptible watermark for text. Peer reviewed at a conference (ICML 2023); the arXiv copy is the authors' own. Tests on one model family; robustness is discussed, not guaranteed.

additions.title: Scalable watermarking for identifying large language model outputs
additions.quote: Watermarking can help identify synthetic text and limit accidental or deliberate misuse
additions.why: Peer-reviewed, open access. Reports a production-ready text watermark that, on the authors' evaluation, preserves text quality, so 'technically feasible' is no longer hypothetical for text. The paper describes its authors' own system; the abstract itself notes watermarking had not been adopted in production before.

additions.title: Can AI-Generated Text be Reliably Detected?
additions.publisher: Sadasivan, Kumar, Balasubramanian, Wang and Feizi, arXiv:2303.11156
additions.quote: while our recursive paraphrasing method can significantly reduce detection rates, it only slightly degrades text quality in many cases
additions.why: The counter-evidence a board should hear: paraphrasing defeats several text detectors, watermark-based ones included, and human-written text can be made to look machine-made. Supports testing robustness and not treating detection as proof. Preprint (version 4, January 2025); attack results on passages of about 300 tokens.

additions.title: Invisible Image Watermarks Are Provably Removable Using Generative AI
additions.quote: we demonstrate that pixel-level invisible watermarks are vulnerable to this regeneration attack
additions.why: Peer reviewed at a conference (NeurIPS 2024). Shows with proofs and tests on four schemes that pixel-level image watermarks can be removed by adding noise and regenerating the image; consistent with Ofcom's cropping finding. Says watermarks that keep the image semantically similar may resist. Laboratory attacks, not measured misuse.

https://ec.europa.eu/newsroom/dae/redire.quote: relying on fingerprinting or logging alone is not considered sufficient

https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu.quote: shall ensure that the outputs of the AI system are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated
shall take the necessary steps in order to comply with Article 50(2) by 2 December 2026

https://www.ofcom.org.uk/siteassets/reso.quote: Attribution measures should be used in combination to tackle the greatest range of deepfakes.

https://www.gov.uk/government/publicatio.quote: some developers and service providers provide labelling services and tools in the UK

https://www.asa.org.uk/news/disclosure-o.quote: There is no blanket legal requirement in the UK to disclose the use of AI in ads

Content Credentials: Strengthening Multimedia Integrity in the Generative AI Era (NSA, ASD, CCCS, NCSC-UK)

rejected.title: Ofcom, Deepfake Defences: Mitigating the Harms of Deceptive Deepfakes (23 July 2024)
rejected.reason: Read. Describes watermarks, metadata and labels in general terms; everything it says on marking is covered in more depth by Deepfake Defences 2, already on the list.

rejected.title: Watermarks in the Sand: Impossibility of Strong Watermarking for Generative Models (Zhang et al.)
rejected.reason: Read (abstract). A theoretical impossibility result under stated assumptions; the two attack papers kept make the same point with tests. Left out to avoid padding.

rejected.reason: Bot check (HTTP 403). No ISO page could be read, so no ISO standard is cited.

brief_check: Nothing read contradicts the brief. The California statute and the Commission guidelines both pair marking with a detection tool, which the brief's 'what good looks like' does not mention. Two reading-list notes are dated: the Commission's Article 50 and Article 111 pages now state they show the EUR-Lex consolidated text as at 27 July 2026, not a 'not yet updated' copy.
